FLAKY TEST FINDER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Which of your tests are actually flaky?

Paste the JUnit XML report from two or more runs of the same suite — reruns you already triggered, or a job that reran on CI. This page groups every test by name and tells you which ones flipped between pass and fail (flaky), which failed every time (broken — a real bug), and which passed every time (stable).

Nothing is uploaded. The XML you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device.

1. Get JUnit XML from two or more runs

Any framework that writes JUnit XML works:

pytest --junitxml=run1.xml         # then run it again for run2.xml
jest --reporters=jest-junit        # needs jest-junit installed
go test ./... 2>&1 | go-junit-report > run.xml
mvn test                           # Surefire writes target/surefire-reports/*.xml automatically

If your CI already reruns failed tests, that rerun report is exactly what you want here — it does not need to contain every test, only the ones it ran.

2. Paste each run's XML

Paste at least two runs and click "Find flaky tests". One run only works for Surefire's own <flakyFailure> elements — everything else needs at least two.

Verdict

Show stable tests too

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py run1.xml run2.xml run3.xml   # exits 1 if any test is flaky
python3 check.py --glob "reports/*.xml"        # or glob a directory of reports
python3 check.py run1.xml run2.xml --json      # machine-readable

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install. It reads local files and makes no network call.

Common questions

How is 'flaky' decided?

A test that failed in at least one run and passed in at least one other run of the same nominal suite is flaky. That is a fact about the reports you gave it, not a guess or a model output — no AI, no heuristics beyond counting pass/fail occurrences per test.

What if my rerun only re-ran the tests that failed?

That is the most common real shape and it is handled: a test does not have to appear in every report to be classified. If it failed in the full run and passed in the rerun-of-failures, it is still counted as flaky using exactly the occurrences it has.

Which test frameworks does this work with?

Anything that emits JUnit XML: pytest (--junitxml), Jest via jest-junit, Go via go-junit-report, PHPUnit, RSpec via RSpecJUnitFormatter, and Maven/Gradle Surefire/Failsafe. Surefire's own <flakyFailure>/<flakyError> elements are also read directly. Even a single Surefire report with retries enabled can surface flakiness this way.

Is my test output uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the XML you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads local files and makes no network call at all.

More: why tests go flaky in CI and what to do about each one, how this compares to BuildPulse, a paid, connected, always-on alternative, or why eyeballing two CI logs gets this wrong once a suite reruns only its failures.

Related: if every check fails in a few seconds with an empty body, first check whether GitHub assigned a runner with the actions runner starvation check — paste the run’s job JSON and it reads runner_id.

Related: once the suite is stable, split it across CI shards by measured duration with the CI test shard balancer — it reads the same JUnit XML and prints the files for each shard.

Related: if tests are stable but line coverage fell on the PR, the coverage drop check compares two Cobertura or JaCoCo reports and names the files that got worse — nothing uploaded.

vs-buildpulse.html.text:
← Flaky Test Finder

Flaky Test Finder vs. BuildPulse

BuildPulse is a paid subscription product that connects to your CI provider — GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Buildkite, and others — through an action or SDK that uploads every build's test results to BuildPulse's servers. It builds a running dashboard of which tests have been flaky across your whole team's history, and can auto-quarantine the worst offenders so they stop blocking merges. Its free tier connects a repository and shows your flakiest tests starting from the first build, with paid plans priced by how many test results you send per day.

That is a genuinely useful job, and it is not this tool's job. This page parses the JUnit-XML reports you paste — nothing is uploaded, there is no account, and nothing is remembered once you close the tab.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have a failed run and its rerun right now — did the same test flip? Flaky Test Finder — paste both reports, get a verdict in seconds, no signup, nothing leaves your device.
Which of our tests have been flaky across the last month of everyone's builds? BuildPulse or a similar connected dashboard — that needs ongoing history across many builds, which a stateless browser page never collects.
I want flaky tests to stop blocking merges automatically, without anyone deciding case by case. BuildPulse's quarantine feature — this tool only classifies what you paste; it does not touch your CI configuration or your test suite.
I don't want to connect my CI or send test data anywhere just to check one flip. Flaky Test Finder — the browser page never makes a network request, and the CLI never phones home either.

The two are not substitutes. A team that wants ongoing, historical, whole-organization flaky-test tracking with automatic quarantine needs a connected, always-on tool like BuildPulse — a page that only looks at whatever you paste into it, once, cannot do that job. A person staring at one red check who already has two reports and wants an answer before signing up for anything does not need a subscription or a CI integration to get it.

Common questions

Should I use Flaky Test Finder or BuildPulse?

They answer the same underlying question — is this test flaky — for different situations. BuildPulse is a paid subscription product that connects to your CI provider (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Buildkite, and others) via an action or SDK that uploads every build's test results to BuildPulse's servers, then builds a historical dashboard across your whole team and auto-quarantines the worst offenders so they stop blocking merges. It answers "which of our tests have been flaky over the last weeks or months, across everyone's builds", continuously, without you doing anything once it is connected. Flaky Test Finder is a free tool with no account and no connection: you paste two or more JUnit-XML reports you already have — say, a failed run and its rerun — and get a deterministic classification in your browser, right now, with nothing sent anywhere. It answers "did this specific test flip between these specific runs", once, for whoever is staring at a red check this minute. If you want an always-on team dashboard with history, BuildPulse's job is not one this page tries to do. If you have two reports in hand and want an answer before signing up for anything, that is what this tool is for.

Does using Flaky Test Finder require connecting my CI or creating an account?

No. There is nothing to connect and nothing to sign up for. The browser page parses the JUnit XML you paste entirely on your own device and never sends it anywhere; the CLI reads local files and makes no network call at all. BuildPulse's own public documentation describes the opposite model for its free tier: connect your repository and its GitHub Action uploads test results to BuildPulse so its dashboard can show your flakiest tests starting from the first build, which is a reasonable design for an always-on team tool, but it does mean your test result data leaves your infrastructure to reach BuildPulse's service.

Does BuildPulse do anything this tool cannot?

Yes — continuous history across many builds and many contributors, automatic quarantine of flaky tests so they stop blocking merges without a person deciding case by case, and integrations with GitHub, Bitbucket, Jira, and Slack for a whole team's workflow, none of which a browser page with no server and no account can do. This tool has no memory between visits, quarantines nothing automatically, and only ever compares the specific reports you paste into it in that session.

Is this page affiliated with BuildPulse?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by BuildPulse. BuildPulse is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on BuildPulse's own public pricing and documentation pages.

vs-eyeballing-two-ci-logs-by-hand.html.text:
← Flaky Test Finder

Flaky Test Finder vs. eyeballing two CI logs by hand

Eyeballing two console logs is the default method, because it needs no tool: open the first failed run, open its rerun, and compare by eye. It works when a suite is small and exactly one test failed. It stops working the moment a suite reruns only its failures — pytest --lf, jest --onlyFailures, and most CI "retry failed tests" features all do this by design — because the second log then contains a different, smaller set of tests than the first, and reading "the rerun looked mostly green" is not the same claim as "every test that failed the first time passed the second time."

Run 1 (full suite, 4 tests)Run 2 (--lf rerun, 2 tests)Verdict
test_login — passednot rerunstable
test_checkout — failed (cart total mismatch)test_checkout — passedflaky — flipped
test_export — failed (export timeout)test_export — failed (same timeout)broken — failed both times
test_search — passednot rerunstable

Eyeballing this pair of logs, both failures look the same shape: "failed in run 1, and run 2 is a rerun of just the failures." The natural read is "the rerun is mostly green, this was probably all flakiness" — which is true of test_checkout and false of test_export, which failed with the identical TimeoutError both times it ran. Pasted into this tool, the two reports are read test-by-test across every run each test appeared in: test_checkout classifies as flaky (1 pass, 1 fail), test_export classifies as broken (2 fails, 0 passes) — a real, consistent failure, not noise. Merging on "the rerun looked fine" ships whatever test_export exists to catch.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have a failed run and its rerun open in two tabs right now — which failures are flaky and which are real? Flaky Test Finder — paste both reports, get a verdict per test in seconds, no guessing which one caught your eye.
The suite only reran its failures, so the second log is smaller — does that mean the missing tests broke? Neither, by hand or here: a test absent from a rerun because it was not retried is not evidence of anything. This tool already treats that as the retry it is, not a missing result.
I want to know if this is the exact same test that has been flaky for weeks, across many past builds. Neither this tool nor eyeballing two logs — that needs history across many runs over time, which two reports pasted once cannot provide. A connected dashboard tool is built for that job.
I have three or more reruns and want to be sure before I mark a test as quarantined. Flaky Test Finder — it accepts any number of reports at once and classifies from all of them together, which gets more reliable with more runs; eyeballing gets slower and more error-prone with each additional log.

Neither method is wrong about small cases: one test, two logs, obviously different failure messages — a person can read that correctly every time. The gap opens exactly where CI already makes eyeballing hardest: a suite with dozens or hundreds of tests, a rerun that only covers the failures, and a reader under time pressure to just get the check green. That is precisely when "mostly green now" and "every specific test that failed actually flipped" stop being the same sentence, and it is the gap this tool exists to close.

Common questions

What does eyeballing two CI logs get wrong?

It conflates two different facts that look identical in a console: a test that failed once and passed on rerun (flaky), and a test that failed the same way in both runs (broken, not flaky). Once a suite reruns only its failed tests -- pytest --lf, jest --onlyFailures, and most CI 'retry failed tests' features all do this -- the second log legitimately contains only a fraction of the first, and a person skimming it tends to read 'mostly green now' as 'must have just been flaky' without checking whether every specific test that failed actually flipped, or whether one of them failed again.

Can you give a concrete example?

A 4-test run fails test_checkout and test_export; test_login and test_search pass. The team reruns only the two failures with --lf. In the rerun, test_checkout passes and test_export fails again with the same TimeoutError. Eyeballing two logs, both failures look the same: 'failed in run 1'. Pasted into this tool, the two reports classify differently: test_checkout is flaky (1 pass, 1 fail across 2 runs), test_export is broken (2 fails, 0 passes across 2 runs) -- a real, consistent failure. Merging past it because 'the rerun looked mostly fine' ships the regression test_export exists to catch.

Is this tool just automating something obvious?

The individual fact -- did this one test flip -- is obvious once you already know to check it test-by-test across every run it appeared in, including the runs where it did not appear. What eyeballing gets wrong is scale and attention, not logic: a report with 40, 200, or 2,000 tests makes 'read every test's status across every run and note which ones appeared in which' the kind of bookkeeping a person skips by pattern-matching on the overall shape of the log instead ('mostly green' or 'still red'). This tool does the same bookkeeping mechanically and exhaustively, so the answer does not depend on which test happened to catch the reader's eye.

Does this replace reading the CI log at all?

No. It replaces the specific step of deciding, test by test, whether a failure is flaky or a real regression. You still need the JUnit-XML reports in hand -- most CI systems already produce or can be configured to produce them -- and you still decide what to do about a broken test once it is correctly identified as broken. This tool only removes the guessing from that one classification step.

why-are-my-tests-flaky-in-ci.html.text:
FLAKY TEST FINDER · GUIDE

Why are my tests flaky in CI?

"Flaky" means a test fails sometimes and passes other times with no code change in between. It is different from a broken test, which fails every time — see the first question below for why that distinction matters before you start debugging anything.

Find out which tests are actually flaky first

Guessing from memory ("I think it's the checkout test") wastes time on the wrong one. Compare two or more runs and let the pass/fail pattern tell you — free, runs in your browser, nothing uploaded.

Open Flaky Test Finder →

Common questions

Why does a test pass locally but fail intermittently in CI?

CI runners are usually slower and more resource-constrained than a laptop, and often run tests in parallel across more workers. That surfaces timing assumptions (a fixed sleep instead of an actual wait condition), shared state between tests running concurrently, and real network or filesystem calls that a local run's warm cache or already-open connection was hiding.

What's the difference between a flaky test and a broken test?

A broken test fails every time under the same conditions — that is a real regression in the code or the test. A flaky test fails sometimes and passes other times with no code change in between — the test or its environment is nondeterministic. Treating a broken test as flaky (retrying until green) ships a real bug; treating a flaky test as broken (blaming the last commit) wastes time bisecting a change that did nothing.

Should I just retry flaky tests until they pass?

As a short-term unblock for a release, sometimes. As a permanent policy, no — a suite where flaky tests are silently retried stops being a signal at all, since a real regression that also happens to race can pass on retry too. Track which tests are flaky and fix the highest-value ones; a rerun-until-green CI step should be a visible, counted exception, not silent default behavior.

How do I find out which of my tests are actually flaky before I start debugging?

Run the suite (or the reruns your CI already does) at least twice and compare pass/fail per test — a test that flips is flaky, a test that fails every time is a real bug. The free Flaky Test Finder tool on this site does exactly that from JUnit XML reports you already have, with no signup and nothing uploaded.

The four causes that account for most flaky tests

1. Timing and race conditions

A fixed sleep(1) instead of waiting for an actual condition (an element to appear, a job to finish, a lock to release) works on a fast machine and fails on a loaded CI runner. Look for hardcoded delays and replace them with a poll-until-true or an explicit wait on the real event.

2. Shared or leaked state between tests

A global variable, a database row, or a file on disk that one test writes and does not clean up can make a later test pass or fail depending on execution order or whether tests run in parallel. This is the most common cause when a test only fails when run alongside the full suite, never in isolation.

3. Real network or filesystem calls

A test that hits a real API, a real DNS lookup, or a real disk write inherits that dependency's own reliability — a slow upstream service, a rate limit, or a transient DNS failure will show up as an intermittent test failure that has nothing to do with your code. Mock the boundary in unit tests; keep real calls to a smaller, explicitly-flagged integration suite.

4. Test order and parallelism assumptions

A test suite that assumes it always runs in file order, or that test IDs are assigned sequentially, breaks the moment a test runner shards or randomizes execution — which most CI systems now do by default to cut wall-clock time. Randomize test order locally on purpose to surface this before CI does.
